blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: A prescription medicine in the United States comes with labeling written for prescribers, and many medicines also carry a text written for patients: a Medication Guide or a patient package insert. The two texts describe the same medicine for two readers, yet public resources rarely hold them side by side. I present PlainPairs, an open corpus built from the openFDA drug label files. Version 0.1.0 holds 35,177 prescription labels that carry a patient text, 21,416 distinct patient texts, 250,829 patient-text segments matched to prescriber sections through their regulatory headings, reading-level measures on both sides, and rule-based counts of plain-language wording. A second source, the National Cancer Institute's cancer information summaries, adds 756 summaries in health-professional and patient versions, in English and Spanish. Measured on the structure of the label, the median Medication Guide reads at grade 8.7 by Flesch-Kincaid and at grade 11.1 by SMOG. The same guides measured on the flattened text that the bulk files serve read about two grades higher, a difference that comes from lost list and heading boundaries. Patient texts address the reader in 41 of every 100 sentences, against 0.2 in prescriber sections. A blind hand check of 100 pairs supports the heading-based alignment for seven of ten heading types. The corpus, its code and its documents are public, and the release keeps texts that show a company copyright mark out of the text tables.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
People who take a prescription medicine in the United States may receive two official texts
about it. One is the prescribing information, written for clinicians. The other, for many
medicines, is a Medication Guide or a patient package insert, written for the person who takes
the medicine. Both are part of the same approved label, and both are public. They are the
closest thing the health system has to a matched pair of texts on one topic for two audiences.

blocks.en:
That pair matters to two research communities. Health communication and health literacy
researchers have long asked whether patient medicine information can be read by the people it
is written for. Low health literacy is associated with worse health outcomes ( Berkman et al., 2011 ) , patients often misread even short instructions on medicine containers ( Davis et al., 2006 ) , and written medicine information has well-known limits as a way to inform
patients ( Shrank and Avorn, 2007 ) . Studies of Medication Guides have repeatedly found them above the
recommended reading level ( Wolf et al., 2006 ; Wolf et al., 2012 ; Jones et al., 2021 ) . Researchers in natural language
processing, in turn, need pairs of expert and lay texts to train and test systems that rewrite
medical language for general readers ( Al-Thanyyan and Azmi, 2021 ) , and the quality of such systems
depends on the pairs they learn from ( Xu et al., 2015 ) .

fields, with no link between a patient text and the prescriber sections that cover the same
ground, no measures, and text that has lost its lists and headings.

blocks.en:
This paper describes PlainPairs, a corpus that fills in those missing parts. It is built from
every label in one openFDA export, keeps the prescription labels that carry a Medication Guide
or a patient package insert, and adds four things to them: 1. Pairing and alignment. Each patient text is cut at its standard headings, and
each segment is matched to the prescriber sections that its heading points to, with a
similarity score for every candidate section. 2. Measures on both sides. Every text and section carries word and sentence
counts, Flesch-Kincaid and SMOG grades, and counts of wording features such as direct
address, commands, percentages and doses. 3. The label’s structure. For labels that DailyMed serves in the same version,
paragraphs, list items and headings are read from the label’s XML, so that reading levels
are measured on the text as it is laid out and not on a flattened string. 4. A second pair of the same kind. Text from the National Cancer Institute’s
cancer information summaries, in health-professional and patient versions, in English and
Spanish.

blocks.en: 2.1 Patient texts in U.S. prescription labeling
blocks.zh: 2.1 美国处方标签中的病人文本

blocks.en:
Two kinds of patient text are part of approved prescription labeling. A Medication Guide is
required for medicines that the Food and Drug Administration judges to pose a serious and significant public health concern.
The regulation asks for nontechnical, understandable language without naming a reading grade,
and it sets headings in a fixed order, such as “What is the most important information I
should know about [the medicine]?”, of which a guide carries those relevant to its product ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2026 ) . A patient package insert is an older and less uniform form, long
required for a few classes of medicines and supplied voluntarily for others. Many labels also
carry Instructions for Use for products such as injectors and inhalers. In 2023 the agency
proposed to replace these forms with a single one-page document, Patient Medication
Information, phased in over five years ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2023 ) . If that rule is made final, a corpus
that follows the labels over time would record the change from the old texts to the new.

blocks.en: 2.2 Readability of patient medicine information
blocks.zh: 2.2 患者医药信息的可读性

blocks.en:
Studies of Medication Guides have measured small sets by hand. Wolf et al. (2006) reviewed all
40 guides issued at the time and found an average reading level of grade 11 to 12 by Lexile
score; none met the federal recommendation of a sixth- to eighth-grade level. A later study
assessed 185 guides, of which seven were at or below grade 8, and tested comprehension with
449 adults ( Wolf et al., 2012 ) . Jones et al. (2021) examined the guides of 53 new molecular entities
approved in 2011, 2013, 2015 and 2017. By Flesch-Kincaid the mean grade was 8.4 and 77% of
the guides met a grade-8 target; by the Fog index and the Fry graph, 11% and 9% did. Other work compared 33 guides with Wikipedia articles ( Candelario et al., 2017 ) , assessed patient materials of risk management programs ( Chan et al., 2018 ) , compared professional and patient information for 16 antifungal medicines
across four regions ( Moore et al., 2023 ) , and tested leaflets for antiseizure medicines in the
United Kingdom ( Noble et al., 2022 ) . A review of 22 leaflet studies noted both the small samples
and the limits of formulas ( Pires et al., 2015 ) . One recent study asked language models to rewrite
agency communications to a lower grade ( Sridharan and Sivaramakrishnan, 2024 ) .

blocks.en:
Two points from this literature shape the corpus. First, readability formulas disagree. Wang et al. (2013) applied several formulas to the same health materials and found differences
of up to five grades on the same text, depending on the formula and on how the text is
prepared. They judged SMOG best suited to health information; Redish (2000) lists what formulas cannot see at all, such as layout and
whether the content answers the reader’s question. PlainPairs therefore reports Flesch-Kincaid
and SMOG together and never one alone. Second, instruments such as the Patient Education
Materials Assessment Tool ( Shoemaker et al., 2014 ) rate understandability and actionability by
hand, including layout and visual aids. The corpus’s wording counts are informed by some of
its text items, but they are not scores on that instrument.

side is a research summary: Cochrane plain-language summaries ( Devaraj et al., 2021 ) , author lay

(2020) aligned the professional and consumer versions of one
publisher’s medical manual. The Spanish CLARA-MeD corpus is the closest in kind: it includes

blocks.en:
For U.S. labels, the nearest prior work is that of Meyer et al. (2023) . They took 5,357
prescription labels from the September 2019 edition of DailyMed, of which 1,437 had a
Medication Guide, and trained a summarization model to generate a guide from the prescribing
information. To prepare the training pairs they cut each guide at six of its standard
questions and aligned each answer to the label in three ways: with the whole label, with label
sections chosen by hand from domain knowledge, and with the single most similar section by
several text-similarity measures, of which BM25 worked best. The alignment in PlainPairs rests
on the same two ideas, a mapping from headings to sections and a similarity score
(Section 4.4 ). Their goal was text generation for regulatory writing, evaluated
with overlap metrics, and their data statement points to DailyMed itself and not to a released
set of pairs. PlainPairs differs in purpose and in what it ships: all labels in scope in a
current export, patient package inserts as well as guides, ten heading types, a hand check of
the mapping, reading-level and wording measures on both sides, and public files with the
rules that built them.

blocks.en: 3.3 Rights and the text switch
blocks.zh: 3.3 权利和文本开关

blocks.en:
openFDA states that its content is in the public domain under a CC0 dedication unless
otherwise noted ( openFDA, 2026 ) . The labels themselves are written by the companies that
market each medicine, and 3,781 of the 35,177 labels in scope (10.7%) show a copyright sign,
the word “copyright” or “all rights reserved” somewhere in their text. I do not know
whether those marks limit reuse of label text, and the corpus does not try to settle the
question. It is built in two layers instead. The record layer holds identifiers, dates,
hashes, lengths, measures, counts and alignment scores, and no text. The text layer holds the
cleaned texts. A switch decides which text rows a release carries: all, only those of labels
with no mark, or none. Version 0.1.0 uses the middle setting, which holds back 68,156 text
rows of marked labels while keeping their record rows. A command in the software rebuilds any
label’s text from the source’s own files and confirms it against the stored hash, so the text
layer can be reproduced by anyone who downloads the same export.

blocks.en: 4.1 Parsing, identity and repeats
blocks.zh: 4.1 分析、身份和重复

blocks.en:
Each label is read from the bulk files and becomes one row. Every section is cleaned of markup
remains and stray spacing with all words kept. Tables arrive as HTML and are stored apart from
the running text, and the copies of tables that the source repeats inside a section’s text are
cut before any measure is taken.

留下并移动间隔,所有文字均保留。 表格以 HTML 格式运抵,并另存
正在运行的文本,以及来源在一节文本中重复的表格副本为
在采取任何措施之前切除。

blocks.en:
A label is identified by its set identifier, which is stable across versions. Naming the
medicine is harder, because only 15,022 of the 35,177 labels carry the source’s product block
with generic names. For the rest, the corpus borrows a medicine key from a label that carries
an identical patient text and does have generic names, and otherwise leaves it empty. As a
result, 16,122 labels have no medicine key, and the count of distinct medicines (1,713) is a
lower bound.

blocks.en:
Many labels share a patient text, because generic products copy the guide of the original
product. Each patient text gets three hashes: exact, loose (ignoring case, punctuation and
symbols), and core (loose, without the closing lines that name the maker and the revision
date). Texts are grouped by the core hash. Reading levels are always reported over distinct
texts, so that a guide used by 40 labels counts once.

blocks.en:

each section in the XML are compared with the words of the bulk file. A section matches when
the two token sequences are identical, or when the Dice overlap ( Dice, 1945 ) of their
token bags, D ⁡ ( A , B ) = 2 ​ | A ∩ B | | A | + | B | , D(A,B)=\frac{2\,|A\cap B|}{|A|+|B|}, (1) is 0.98 or more. A third class covers sections where the bulk file repeats a subsection that
the XML holds once.

blocks.en: 4.5 Rule-based counts of wording

blocks.en:
The corpus counts wording features that the plain-language literature treats as signs of text

This section reports four checks: that the XML and the bulk files hold the same words, how
much the measurement basis changes reading levels, how the wording counts were checked, and

blocks.en: 6.1 The same words in both sources

blocks.en:
Measures from structure are only meaningful if the XML holds the same text as the bulk file.
Of the 12,857 distinct patient texts in current , 12,848 match word for word, 6 match at a
Dice overlap of 0.98 or more, and 3 belong to the class where the bulk file repeats a
subsection. Labels where a patient text did not match are in unlisted by construction.

depending on the section. Word counts taken from the flattened text are too high for those
sections, and the measures from structure are not affected.

blocks.en: 6.2 Structure against flattened text

blocks.en:
Figure 2 compares the two bases on the same 7,088 distinct Medication Guides.
Measured on structure, the median guide has 134 sentences; measured on the flattened text it
has 98, because the 56 list items of the median guide are joined into fewer, longer units.
The Flesch-Kincaid grade from the flattened text is higher in 98.9% of guides, by a median of
1.94 grades (middle half 1.17 to 2.76), and the SMOG grade is higher by a median of 1.63. For
patient package inserts the median differences are 1.44 and 1.19 grades.

blocks.en:
To check the mapping of headings to sections, I drew 100 segment pairs with a fixed seed, 10

blocks.en: 7.1 Reading levels of patient texts
blocks.zh: 7.1 阅读病历

blocks.en:
Table 8 gives reading levels over distinct texts. In current , measured on
structure, the median Medication Guide reads at grade 8.67 by Flesch-Kincaid (middle half 7.88
to 9.48) and at grade 11.10 by SMOG. By Flesch-Kincaid, 71.9% of guides are above grade 8; by
SMOG, 99.2% are. Patient package inserts are close to the guides: grade 8.58 and 11.21.
blocks.zh:
表8列出了不同文本的阅读水平。 以当前值计量
Flesch-Kincaid在8.67年级读作中位数《药物指南》(中位数7.88)
至9.48),11.10年级由SMOG完成. 根据Flesch-Kincaid,71.9%的导游在8年级以上;
SMOG,99.2%为. 患者包插入器接近向导:8.58级和11.21级.

blocks.en:
Whether Medication Guides meet a grade-8 target therefore depends on the formula. On
Flesch-Kincaid, more than a quarter do and the median is within a grade of the target. On

blocks.en: This section lists what limits the claims in this paper, starting with the largest.

blocks.en:

blocks.en: 10 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 10. 结论

blocks.en:
PlainPairs puts the two official texts of U.S. prescription medicines side by side: 35,177
labels, 21,416 distinct patient texts, and 250,829 segments matched to prescriber sections,
with measures and wording counts on both sides and a second pair from cancer summaries. The
first release shows that Medication Guides sit near grade 9 on one common formula and near
grade 11 on another, that the flattened text of the bulk files overstates both by one to two
grades, and that patient texts address the reader directly while leaving out nearly all the
numbers the prescriber is given. I expect the corpus to be useful for work on how medicine
information is worded for patients, on automatic rewriting of medical text, and, if the
proposed one-page patient document becomes a rule, on how patient labeling changes.

PlainPairs将美国两种处方药的官方文本并列:35,177
标签,21,416份不同的病历,250,829个部分与处方部分相匹配,
措施与措辞在两边都算数,从癌症摘要中得出第二对。 那个
第一次发布表明,药品指南在一个共同公式上坐在接近9年级的地方,而且接近
11年级在另一年级, 平整的文本 散装文件的文字 超标了两个 1到2
并且病人的文本直接与读者联系,而忽略了几乎所有
给出处方符的号码。 我期望这本书能帮助研究医学
信息是针对病人的,关于医疗文本的自动改写,如果
提议用一页的病人文件成为关于病人标签如何改变的规则。
